item.title: Year-Round Lagoon Resorts Enter Mixed-Use Development Playbook
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
St. Charles advances sale of 19.5 acres for Missouri's first indoor lagoon resort, adding year-round beach amenity to $350 million riverfront district.

The post Year-Round Lagoon Resorts Enter Mixed-Use Development Playbook appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
St. Charles, Missouri has given preliminary approval to sell 19.5 acres of city-owned riverfront land for $4.15 million to Lux Haven Group LLC, a local developer proposing an enclosed lagoon beach resort and condominium complex. Beach Club at Riverpointe would feature a three-quarter-acre indoor lagoon under a climate-controlled dome, 150 to 315 condos, and 35,000 to 50,000 square feet of commercial space in its first phase. The project would be the first year-round indoor lagoon resort in Missouri. Final approval could come as soon as November 17.

Later phases would add a 200-room hotel, additional residential development, golf amenities, and other resort features. Marketing materials describe white sand, warm water, cabanas, a swim-up bar, waterfall, spa, and public access through day passes and memberships. Developer Lux Haven, led by St. Charles real estate investor William Schmitt, plans to break ground in spring 2027, open the beach later that year, and deliver first residential units in 2028. Development costs were not disclosed.

Beach Club joins the city’s $350 million Riverpointe district, a 120-acre riverfront redevelopment zone near Interstate 70 that already includes Chicken N Pickle and has a dual-branded hotel and at least 200 apartments under development by Edward Rose Properties. The land sale is contingent on additional agreements and would include tax incentives such as Community Improvement District and Transportation Development District designations, plus a temporary Chapter 100 property tax abatement. The project represents a new amenity category for mixed-use developments seeking to differentiate residential offerings in second-tier markets.

St. Louis Business Journal
St. Charles Advances $4.15M Land Sale as Developer Proposes Missouri's First Indoor Lagoon Resort

item.title: AI In Property Management Has a Ground-Truth Problem
item.dc:creator: Mike Laurie
item.description:
AI in property management needs more than connected data: verified building information, clear provenance and visible uncertainty are essential for trust.

The post AI In Property Management Has a Ground-Truth Problem appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence has a remarkable ability to consume building information. Give it drawings, specifications, inspection reports, maintenance records, leases, photographs and spreadsheets, and it will extract facts at a speed no human team could match.

Much of the current conversation about AI agents in property management turns on the need for a coherent data structure underneath them, so that agents working across maintenance, leasing and operations can reconcile their outputs instead of each acting on a partial view. I agree with that entirely. But a common schema solves only one part of the problem. It can organize the information. It cannot, by itself, tell us whether that information still describes the physical building.

That distinction is not hypothetical. Existing buildings are full of records that disagree with each other. One drawing puts a wall in one location and a later plan puts it somewhere else. The lease abstract carries one area and the measurement carries another. An equipment schedule lists a unit that was replaced years ago and never removed from the list. AI can read all of it. It still needs some way to know which version is true.

The physical world is the final authority

In my line of work we spend a great deal of time resolving exactly these discrepancies, and the answer is usually old fashioned. Go back to the building. Measure it, look at it, identify the equipment, confirm the space, record the condition.

The tools have changed enormously. LiDAR, mobile scanning, 360 degree imagery and computer vision have made verification faster, cheaper and far richer than it was even five years ago. The principle has not changed at all. For a physical asset, the physical world is still the only authority that settles an argument.

This is where I think the industry’s mental model of the stack is incomplete. The chain is usually described as software systems, then a common data model, then an AI agent. For existing buildings it needs one more layer underneath: the physical building, then verified ground truth, then the connected data structure, then AI. That extra step is the least visible part of the architecture and the part that lets everything above it earn trust. Without it, an outdated drawing, a stale equipment schedule and a current maintenance record all populate the same beautifully organized schema, and the result is wrong in a format that looks authoritative.

Provenance is about to matter a great deal

As AI takes a larger role in real estate decisions, I expect to hear far more about provenance. Where did this number come from? Who established it? Which standard was applied? When was it last verified? Has the building changed since then?

Those questions are familiar to anyone who works in building measurement, and they become considerably more important once machines are assembling answers from thousands of sources at once. A building record should not simply hold a value. It should hold enough context to explain why that value deserves to be believed.

My expert witness work has made this unusually vivid. Disputes involving floor area or measurement standards are almost never resolved by finding one more spreadsheet. They are resolved by understanding the source documents, the standard that applied, the physical conditions at the time and the method used to arrive at the number. AI can help organize that evidence and it can find inconsistencies a person would miss. But evidence and truth are not the same thing, and the distinction is going to matter well beyond litigation. It will matter in acquisitions, in leasing, in capital planning and in any decision where building data carries financial weight.

Let it say “I don’t know”

We have all become accustomed to software returning an answer. Building AI is going to need a different habit.

Sometimes the most useful answer is that the system does not know. Or that it found two conflicting sources. Or that nothing has been verified since the renovation. That is not a weakness in the product. It is the feature that makes the rest of it credible.

A system worth trusting should maintain confidence levels, surface conflicts rather than resolving them silently, and build a verification queue that someone actually works through. Over time every inspection, scan, service call and capital project improves the record. The result is never a perfect database, because buildings are too dynamic for that. What we can realistically build is a building record whose uncertainty is visible and managed rather than hidden.

The preparation happens in mechanical rooms

There is a great deal of talk about getting data ready for AI, and in most industries that means cleaning databases. In real estate it cannot mean only that, because we are dealing with physical assets.

Some of the most valuable AI preparation in this industry is going to happen in mechanical rooms, on rooftops, in tenant spaces and in parking garages, where the digital record finally meets the actual building. It is unglamorous work and it is not what anyone puts in a funding announcement.

Whoever solves that connection between physical truth and machine intelligence will have built something more valuable than another dataset. They will have built trust. Without it, talking to a building stays an impressive demonstration rather than a reliable way to run real estate.

The post AI In Property Management Has a Ground-Truth Problem appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Fatal Brooklyn Collapse Triggers Citywide Construction Site Audit
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
New York will inspect 100 construction sites after a Brooklyn building collapse killed eight people and injured 19 near an active development project.

The post Fatal Brooklyn Collapse Triggers Citywide Construction Site Audit appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
A three-story residential building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn collapsed Wednesday afternoon, killing at least eight people and injuring 19 others. The structure fell into an excavation pit created by construction at an adjacent property at 2625 Bedford Avenue, where a one-story building was being converted into a nine-unit apartment complex. Emergency crews continued extracting victims from the rubble hours after the 4:30 p.m. collapse, with one injured person remaining in critical condition as of Thursday afternoon. Among the dead were two children and two construction workers.

New York City officials announced a sweep of approximately 100 construction sites connected to the five entities involved in the adjacent development project. The Department of Buildings had issued a stop-work order for the Bedford Avenue site in March, but a follow-up inspection found the original building had already been demolished, resulting in a $10,000 fine. DOB Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said the agency is conducting a “whole-of-government investigation” while continuing to document evidence as debris is cleared. The collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue contained four apartment units and is owned by Isolag Realty Corp., which acquired the property in 2024.

The incident adds to mounting concerns about construction oversight in New York, where the city’s building boom has strained inspection resources. The planned audit of 100 sites represents one of the largest enforcement actions triggered by a single incident in recent years. Mayor Mamdani promised full accountability for any responsible parties, though the exact cause of the collapse remained under investigation as of Thursday.

item.title: New York’s Right of First Refusal Law Adds Transaction Delays for Distressed Multifamily
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
New York's COPA law grants nonprofits first refusal rights on 2,100 multifamily buildings, adding transaction delays critics say discourage private investment.

The post New York’s Right of First Refusal Law Adds Transaction Delays for Distressed Multifamily appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act into law on Tuesday, requiring owners of certain multifamily buildings to notify the city before selling and grant nonprofits a right of first refusal. COPA takes effect in November 2027 and applies to roughly 2,100 buildings, including distressed properties with four or more units and smaller buildings subject to affordability restrictions. Eligible nonprofits have 20 days to submit a statement of interest and 70 days to make an initial offer. If an owner receives a competing bid from a private buyer, the nonprofit retains a right of first refusal.

City Council member Sandy Nurse, the bill’s lead sponsor, pushed the legislation through after former Mayor Eric Adams vetoed a broader version in December 2025. The original proposal would have covered 10,000 buildings. Nurse argued the city cannot build its way out of the housing crisis and must preserve existing stock. Manhattan Institute senior fellow John Ketcham countered that the law assumes nonprofit ownership is superior to private ownership without evidence that nonprofits manage maintenance or tenant relations better than private landlords.

A 2025 report from New York University’s Furman Center warned that opportunity-to-purchase laws impose timing delays and legal costs that can discourage investment, particularly in softer markets. Real Deal analyst Erik Engquist noted that nonprofits capable of acquiring distressed buildings already had access to them without the mandate, and COPA simply adds process layers rather than improving acquisition economics. The law follows the Mamdani administration’s rent freeze, which took effect last month, continuing a pattern of regulatory expansion in the city’s housing market.

item.title: California Wealth Tax Defeat Unlocks Deals as Luxury Buyers Return
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
California luxury agents report buyer activity resuming after voters rejected a billionaire wealth tax that had frozen high-end residential deals.

The post California Wealth Tax Defeat Unlocks Deals as Luxury Buyers Return appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
California voters rejected Proposition 40 on Monday, a measure that would have imposed a one-time 5 percent tax on individuals with net worth exceeding $1 billion. The Associated Press called the race with 52.8 percent voting no and 47.2 percent in favor. High-end residential agents reported immediate client activity following the announcement, with showing requests and transaction approvals coming in from buyers who had paused plans. Aaron Kirman of Christie’s International Real Estate Southern California said three of his five billionaire clients contacted him to restart deals in Los Angeles and Atherton, California.

Agents said the tax proposal froze activity across the luxury market, affecting properties priced at $5 million and above as multi-millionaires worried about future levies. The measure drew opposition from commercial real estate figures including Marcus & Millichap founder George Marcus, The Wonderful Company’s Stewart Resnick, and Ducks owner Henry Samueli, who funded campaigns against it. Los Angeles County and San Francisco voted in favor of the tax at roughly 55 percent and 56 percent respectively, while Orange County rejected it 59 percent to 41 percent. Douglas Elliman agent Cory Weiss received two showing requests for his West Hollywood Edition penthouse listing the evening results were announced.

High-end residential brokers view the defeat as relief for a market already strained by Los Angeles’s mansion tax, which took effect in 2023 and applies to sales above certain thresholds. Newmark Estates partner Steven Schaefer said clients who considered leaving California have called to reconsider those plans. Compass’s Carl Gambino cautioned that ultra-wealthy buyers remain wary of future tax measures despite the outcome. A separate ballot measure, Proposition 42, passed and bars new state taxes on financial assets and business interests, though real estate remains taxable.

The mansion tax continues to complicate transactions for sellers who purchased during the pandemic at low interest rates and now face higher borrowing costs plus the additional levy. Gambino described deals falling apart as buyers struggle to justify the combined expense of elevated rates and the tax. Agents pointed to maintenance spending and related services that billionaire property owners support, arguing the tax’s defeat preserves economic activity tied to high-end real estate. Some brokers reported increased call volume for properties above $5 million in the final weekend before the election.

Real Estate Reversal? Client Calls Pour in with Billionaire Tax’s Defeat

item.title: Secondaries Boom Offers Exit Path for Stranded Real Estate Capital
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Blackstone targets $3 billion for a real estate secondaries fund as liquidity pressures drive managers and LPs to sell stakes at discounts.

The post Secondaries Boom Offers Exit Path for Stranded Real Estate Capital appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Blackstone is raising at least $3 billion for a new fund through its Strategic Partners division to buy stakes in other asset managers’ real estate vehicles. The fund will target interests in core real estate funds, acquiring them at discounts to net asset value, with a focus on data center, rental housing and industrial assets. Strategic Partners raised $2.6 billion for a similar fund in 2023.

The fundraising comes as limited partners and asset managers search for liquidity after years of deal drought. The Federal Reserve’s rate increases starting in 2022 slowed transactions across commercial real estate, while the pandemic’s impact on office buildings added further pressure. Real estate secondaries deals led by fund managers reached $14.5 billion last year, up 60% from the prior year, according to Ares Management.

Continuation vehicles have become a preferred tool for managers seeking to retain high-performing assets while providing exits to investors. Private-asset firms have used these structures to extend hold periods on properties in logistics, data centers and senior housing. Ares projects real estate secondaries volumes to double over the next several years as the gap between fundraising and distribution persists.

item.title: Did the Binance Heist Take the Last Air Out of Real Estate Tokenization?
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Blockchain can’t search title or inspect buildings

The post Did the Binance Heist Take the Last Air Out of Real Estate Tokenization? appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
2 days 23 hr agoNov. 11, 2026 5:13 pm

My inbox used to carry a tokenized real estate pitch most weeks. Fractional ownership of a rental portfolio, a deed recorded as an NFT, a coin backed by self-storage. Those have essentially stopped arriving, and what happened at Binance last month makes their return less likely rather than more.

Hackers took $6.3 billion from the world’s largest crypto exchange on October 29, the biggest digital asset theft ever recorded. Binance halted deposits and withdrawals, its co-chief executive pledged to cover the losses, and the company brought in outside cybersecurity reviewers. Bitcoin fell to around $76,400 in the days after. Crypto hacks have taken more than $22.3 billion since 2021, according to Chainalysis, but nothing at this scale had hit an exchange this central to the market. This has reportedly made some rethink the role of cypto in their portfolios as well as how and why tokenization should be used.

Property was always the laggard in tokenization, and private asset owners are now reassessing the whole category. Treasuries and private credit have scaled on-chain. Real estate has not, because the slow parts of a property transaction are slow for reasons a token does not address. Title has to be searched. Condition has to be inspected. Someone has to manage the building. Anyone pitching a blockchain solution for a closing now has to answer for the hack as well, and the answer is not simple.

Binance attributed the breach to North Korea and said the campaign began when one of its engineers was contacted through a job hunting platform by someone posing as a project director. The engineer was interviewed by a person claiming to run a company that did not exist, shown personal photos and social accounts to establish credibility, and asked to download an assignment containing malicious code. Binance called the approach more advanced and deceptive than anything it had seen.

AI makes that kind of attack cheaper to run at scale, generating convincing personas, writing the code, and handling the correspondence, and exchanges are now asking whether their own internal AI systems create new openings rather than closing them. AI also makes mistakes on its own, which is a separate problem that points the same direction. Systems that can reverse a transaction, freeze a transfer, or require a human signature start looking like features instead of overhead.

Quantum computing is the longer-term concern and the timeline keeps shortening. Research published this year cut the estimated resources needed to break the cryptography securing most major chains by roughly twentyfold. Bitcoin merged its first quantum-resistant address proposal in February and Ethereum formed a post-quantum team in January. Expert estimates now cluster between 2029 and the mid-2030s, and some think sooner. If a capable machine arrives before the migration finishes, the security promise underneath distributed ledgers goes with it.

Blockchains were supposed to strip the intermediaries out of a property transaction and leave something faster and cheaper behind. What the past two weeks suggest is that those intermediaries were doing more than adding cost. They were absorbing risk, and the industry now rebuilding that capacity in software is making the case better than any skeptic could.

Writing this will almost certainly put a few tokenization pitches back in my inbox. I guess I might have missed them after all.

The post Did the Binance Heist Take the Last Air Out of Real Estate Tokenization? appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Lenders Have Adopted AI Everywhere But Still Don’t Trust Its Decision Making
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Commercial mortgage lenders are adopting AI to accelerate underwriting, but fragmented data, weak audit trails, and trust gaps still limit credit decisions.

The post Lenders Have Adopted AI Everywhere But Still Don’t Trust Its Decision Making appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Commercial mortgage lenders are working through a heavy year. Roughly $875 billion in commercial mortgages come due in 2026 against originations forecast near $805.5 billion, which means a large volume of refinancing has to be underwritten by teams that were not staffed for it. Pressure like that tends to push technology adoption faster than it otherwise would move.

It has. A market study found 79 percent of financial institutions running AI pilots or operating AI inside lending workflows by July 2026, up from 34 percent in late 2025. That is a steeper adoption curve than online lending, mobile lending, or statistical automated underwriting ever produced.

Where the technology has earned its place is in the document work that occupies the front end of every loan. Converting an offering memorandum, a rent roll, and a trailing twelve into a populated underwriting model has always been the most expensive manual step in a lending shop, and it is exactly the kind of extraction AI handles well. Another study found institutions running purpose-built underwriting platforms reporting 40 to 60 percent reductions in analyst time per commercial loan, with application-to-decision timelines collapsing from the traditional five to ten business days down to 24 to 48 hours. Banks deploying AI underwriting have reported time-to-decision compression of 50 to 75 percent.

Portfolio surveillance has benefited similarly. Covenant monitoring, financial variance analysis, and insurance review are recurring obligations across a loan book that nobody enjoys doing manually, and automating them lets a servicing team watch more loans more closely than headcount would otherwise allow.

Trust is where the progress stops, and the distance between usage and reliance is striking. A CRE Industry Pulse Check found 66 percent of commercial real estate professionals using AI weekly or daily, while only 5 percent said they trusted it enough to inform an actual deal decision. More than half use it for support while explicitly excluding it from final decisions, and another 17 percent use it only with heavy verification.

That caution reflects a specific requirement rather than general skepticism. Institutional credit committees need to know where a number came from, and a well-formatted model that cannot be traced back to a source document fails that test regardless of how fast it was produced. Lenders have increasingly begun treating untraceable data as financial risk, which means deal teams relying on unverified outputs face longer credit reviews, heavier manual audits, and a higher cost of capital rather than a faster process.

Regulation reinforces that position. The Equal Credit Opportunity Act and the Community Reinvestment Act require lending decisions to be explainable and free of discriminatory patterns, and the OCC, FDIC, and CFPB have all signaled that AI-assisted credit decisions remain subject to those standards. A model that produces a defensible answer without a defensible explanation does not satisfy an examiner.

Underneath both problems sits data that was never organized for this. Deloitte’s 2026 Commercial Real Estate Outlook found more than 60 percent of CRE finance organizations citing data fragmentation and manual reconciliation as their primary obstacle to operational efficiency. A loan generates underwriting memos, borrower correspondence, covenant documentation, insurance reviews, and internal credit discussions across its life, and those artifacts typically live in systems that have no relationship to one another.

JLL’s 2026 Global Real Estate Investor AI Survey, released this week, found that readiness determines outcomes more than tooling does. Among investors whose data is not AI-ready, 59 percent struggle to realize the benefits they expected, against 21 percent of those whose data is ready. The survey covered 837 senior decision makers at firms with at least $1 billion in assets under management across twelve countries.

The same survey points to something lenders may find uncomfortable about speed as a strategy. Investors told JLL their top AI priorities were investment outperformance and proprietary analytics in capital deployment, and those were the areas producing the weakest results. The strongest results came from asset and property management, which respondents had ranked as a lower priority. JLL’s explanation has to do with where competition sits. When every bidder underwrites faster using similar tools against similar purchased data, nobody pulls ahead and the seller captures the benefit.

Lending works the same way. Faster time to decision is a real advantage while competitors are slower and stops being one when they catch up, which has already started to happen. What does not get competed away is a lender’s own loan performance history, its relationships, and its accumulated judgment about which borrowers and which markets have worked out.

Getting value from those assets requires more than an enterprise license, and relatively few firms have done that work. JLL found 83 percent of investors with at least one AI activity scaled or fully embedded, and 81 percent of deployments running on enterprise large language models. Only 15 percent had built custom agentic workflows across all their use cases, and one in five had built none anywhere. Broad access through a general-purpose tool does not change how work gets done.

The architecture that appears to be emerging in credit is deliberately mixed. Speaking at Ai4 2026 in Las Vegas, Pranjal Daga, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Accend, argued that a powerful language model alone is not sufficient for high-stakes credit decisions, and that the next stage of commercial lending depends less on adding individual tools than on connecting the underwriting process through a common intelligence layer. What that produces is a hybrid rather than an autonomous system, with AI agents handling selected tasks, conventional software performing exact calculations, verification systems checking outputs, and people responsible for judgment and exceptions.

Lenders building toward AI led decision making are working on the parts that take longest, which are the data connections and the audit trails rather than the models themselves. The firms that get there will be able to move quickly on a deal and explain every number in the file, which is what a credit committee has always wanted and what the current generation of general-purpose tools has not delivered on its own.

The post Lenders Have Adopted AI Everywhere But Still Don’t Trust Its Decision Making appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Blackstone’s Nontraded REIT Books $497M in Impairments While Pivoting to Data Centers
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
BREIT posts $497M in third-quarter impairments on multifamily and office assets while deploying $9B into data centers through QTS.

The post Blackstone’s Nontraded REIT Books $497M in Impairments While Pivoting to Data Centers appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Blackstone Real Estate Income Trust recorded $496.7 million in impairment charges during the third quarter, up from $27.4 million a year earlier. The charges covered 13 rental housing properties, one office building, and single-family rentals, plus $43 million in write-downs for assets held for sale. BREIT did not disclose which properties triggered the impairments. Despite the charges, the nontraded REIT posted a 2% return for the quarter and 7.3% year-to-date, with subscriptions up roughly 40% from last year.

BREIT deployed $3.4 billion into preleased data center developments through QTS in the third quarter, bringing its 2024 investment in the sector to approximately $9 billion. The fund now holds a 34.8% stake in QTS, the data center operator Blackstone took private in 2021. Data centers now represent 29% of BREIT’s real estate value, exceeding its 20% industrial allocation and 17% multifamily weighting. The fund sold $7 billion in noncore assets this year, including its remaining self-storage and manufactured housing portfolios.

BREIT sold 65 rental housing properties, nine industrial assets, and one office building in the quarter for $2 billion, generating a $366.1 million realized gain that partially offset the impairment charges. Total assets under management declined from $98.6 billion at year-end 2023 to $88.9 billion at the end of September. Since inception, BREIT has delivered a 9.3% annualized net return, about 55% higher than publicly traded REITs. Management attributed its optimism to constrained supply across property sectors, arguing that portfolios built on cash flow growth can perform even as rates remain elevated.

item.title: Smart Buildings Need Smart Elevators But Most Owners Are Putting Off Upgrading Them
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Aging U.S. office buildings face urgent elevator modernization needs as owners balance reliability, smart technology, and capital costs.

The post Smart Buildings Need Smart Elevators But Most Owners Are Putting Off Upgrading Them appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The commercial building stock in the United States is older than most portfolio conversations acknowledge. JLL data puts 68 percent of national office inventory as built before 2000, and in many gateway cities more than 70 percent of space is at least 30 years old. The median office building that traded in the first quarter of 2026 was 39 years old, up from 22 in 2000.

Equipment inside those buildings is aging on the same schedule, and vertical transportation is approaching a point where a lot of it needs attention simultaneously. “Nine million of the world’s 23 million elevators are already 15 to 20 years old, that’s right at the age where refurbishment is recommended,” said Joseph Armas, President of Otis Americas. More than a million of those units are in the United States and Canada.

The timing is awkward. Owners carrying buildings through a period of compressed valuations and expensive debt are not looking for capital projects, and elevator modernization is a meaningful one. What most are looking for instead is a way to defer the full expense without letting the equipment degrade to the point where it becomes a tenant problem.

Partial upgrades can buy real time. Replacing a controller, updating a drive, or improving door operation addresses the components most likely to fail without touching the machine or the cab. Armas is direct about what that purchases and what it does not. “That 15-year-old equipment might be able to have its life extended by five to seven years but the owners still need to be thinking about upgrading,” he said.

Deciding when to move from maintenance to modernization depends on what has actually been going wrong. An elevator with occasional mechanical issues is a different asset than one with recurring electrical faults, and the distinction matters because electrical problems tend to indicate the control system has reached the end of its useful life. “The performance history of the elevator is really important,” Armas said. “Are there electrical failures as well as mechanical? If so, you might want to pursue a larger modernization.” Shutdown frequency and duration belong in that analysis as well, since the cost of a building with unreliable vertical transportation shows up in tenant relationships before it shows up in a repair invoice.

There is a second reason the modernization question has gotten more pressing, which has to do with what buildings are being asked to do. Owners investing in building management systems, access control, and occupancy analytics are connecting systems that were never designed to talk to each other, and legacy elevator controllers generally cannot participate.

“We are the spine of the building so we have to be able to integrate with everything,” Armas said. “That can only happen if the elevators get modernized.” A destination dispatch system that cannot read from access control is solving a smaller problem than it could be. An occupancy platform that cannot see elevator traffic is missing the most reliable signal available about how people move through a property.

AI has raised the hardware requirement further. Dispatch algorithms that respond to a call button need very little processing. Systems that anticipate demand need considerably more, along with access to data from outside the elevator itself.

“AI is requiring elevators to have more compute,” Armas said. “They need to know how many people are likely going to be using the elevator, where they are coming from, and how many other elevators are there.” Running that calculation continuously across a bank of elevators in a high-rise is a different computational problem than the equipment installed in 2008 was built to handle.

The same technology is improving how owners plan the work. Modernization decisions have historically been made reactively, triggered by a failure or a code requirement, with limited visibility into what else in the system was approaching the end of its life. Performance data collected continuously changes what can be planned in advance.

“AI is starting to add an intelligence layer that can help the building team and our teams design better operations,” Armas said. “Now it will be able to give a roadmap for any upgrades that would help the building.” A sequenced plan that identifies which components need replacement in which order lets an owner phase the capital rather than absorbing it at once.

Prediction also changes day-to-day operation in ways that matter for buildings running at or near capacity. An elevator system aware of a scheduled event on an upper floor can position cars before attendees arrive and again when the event ends, rather than responding to a surge after it has already formed. Otis has applied that kind of analysis outside the equipment itself, including for a New York finance firm whose employees were consistently returning late from lunch. The traffic data showed the elevators could not handle the noon rush, and the recommendation was a 20 percent lunch discount offered 45 minutes before the peak.

Demand on these systems is not easing. Cities are densifying, office attendance has been climbing on peak midweek days, and the buildings absorbing that traffic are largely the same ones whose equipment is reaching the age where modernization gets recommended.

The post Smart Buildings Need Smart Elevators But Most Owners Are Putting Off Upgrading Them appeared first on Propmodo.
